common_name: Kyoto Dwarf Mondo Grass (Miniature Super-Dwarf Mondo Grass)

planting.note: Plant small divisions or plugs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Kyoto Dwarf grows extremely slowly, so set plugs closer together than standard mondo grass if a solid carpet is wanted within a few seasons.

directions: Plant divisions in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, keeping the planting consistently watered while the tiny tufts knit together into a mat. Kyoto Dwarf is the smallest form of mondo grass in general cultivation, forming dense tufts of thread-fine, dark green, grass-like foliage that rarely exceeds 2 inches tall, far shorter than standard mondo grass, and it spreads by short rhizomes at a notably slow pace. Its diminutive scale makes it a favorite for filling the joints between stepping stones and pavers, edging small shade beds, and miniature or Japanese-style gardens where a finer, lower texture than standard mondo or liriope is wanted. It is evergreen, deer resistant, and tolerant of light foot traffic once established, but division and fresh planting are the only practical way to fill an area quickly, since growth from seed is impractically slow for most gardeners.

common_name: Snow N Summer Asiatic Jasmine (Variegated White-Splashed Groundcover)

planting.note: Plant container-grown plants or rooted cuttings in spring or fall in well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Snow N Summer colors up brightest with a few hours of direct sun but tolerates the same dry shade conditions as plain green asiatic jasmine.

directions: Plant in well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun, and mulch and water regularly until the low, twining stems knit together into a solid mat. Snow N Summer is a variegated sport of Asiatic jasmine bearing small, glossy leaves heavily splashed in white and cream over green, with new growth often flushed pink in cool weather, giving the groundcover noticeably brighter, more varied color than the plain species. It shares the same dense, weed-suppressing, low-maintenance habit prized in Asiatic jasmine, making it useful for lightening dry shade under trees, slopes, and other spots where mowing is impractical, though its variegated leaves are somewhat less vigorous and slower to fill in than solid green Asiatic jasmine. Shear back hard in early spring every couple of years to remove old woody growth and encourage dense, colorful new foliage, and watch for any all-green reverted shoots, cutting them out to keep the planting true to type.

planting.note: Set out transplants after the last frost into partial shade to partial sun in fertile, well-drained soil; Bounce is a downy-mildew-resistant impatiens hybrid bred to replace traditional Impatiens walleriana in beds where the disease has been a problem.

directions: Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in partial shade to partial sun, and feed and water regularly to keep the vigorous, well-branched mounds blooming without interruption. Bounce Lilac is a vegetatively propagated interspecific impatiens hybrid bred with resistance to impatiens downy mildew, the disease that devastated traditional bedding impatiens plantings, while keeping the classic look and shade performance gardeners expect from Impatiens walleriana, covering its mounded habit in soft lavender-lilac flowers from spring through frost. It rebounds quickly after a rain or an accidental broken stem, springing back into full, tidy bloom within days, a trait that gave the series its name. Give it more consistent moisture than SunPatiens types, since Bounce is bred primarily for shade and part-sun performance rather than full-sun heat tolerance, and pinch leggy stems in midsummer to keep plantings dense.
sources: Selecta One — Bounce Impatiens series notes
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Bedding Plant Trials

planting.note: Set out transplants after the last frost in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Illumination Flame is a sterile intergeneric hybrid grown from cuttings, not seed, and it flowers continuously without needing to be deadheaded for seed removal.

directions: Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, providing afternoon shade and consistent moisture where summers are hottest. Illumination Flame is part of the Digiplexis group, a race of sterile intergeneric hybrids between common foxglove (Digitalis purpurea) and the Canary Island shrub foxglove (Isoplexis canariensis), combining the tall spike form of foxglove with a shrubbier, longer-lived, repeat-flowering habit; its tubular flowers open in warm flame-orange shading to rose-pink toward the spike tip and, because the plant is sterile, it channels its energy into producing new flowering spikes all season instead of setting seed. It behaves as a short-lived tender perennial, reliably overwintering outdoors only in the mildest zones, but performs as a long-blooming summer annual almost everywhere else. Deadhead spent spikes to the base to encourage fresh flowering stems, and note that, like other foxgloves, all parts are toxic if ingested.

common_name: Santa Cruz Sunset Begonia (Cascading Orange-Red Bolivian Begonia)

planting.note: Set out transplants or tubers after the last frost into partial shade to morning sun in rich, well-drained soil; Santa Cruz Sunset is grown as a cascading hanging-basket or container plant and does not need pinching to flower heavily.

directions: Plant in rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to gentle morning sun, and keep the shallow root system evenly moist without letting the crown sit in standing water. Santa Cruz Sunset belongs to a series of Begonia boliviensis hybrids bred for a trailing, cascading habit that spills gracefully over the edge of a hanging basket or raised container, bearing narrow, pointed leaves and a nonstop flush of pendant, elongated, single flowers in fiery orange-red from late spring through frost. Unlike fibrous or tuberous bedding begonias grown for mounded garden beds, this Bolivian species is best displayed at eye level or overhead where its cascading stems and bright color can be seen from below. It holds up to heat and light rain far better than old-fashioned tuberous begonias, but still prefers a spot sheltered from the most intense midday sun and from strong wind, which can shred the relatively thin, brittle stems.
